issue_context.title: BUG: Series.str.find with pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()) produces unexpected results
issue_context.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> a = pd.Series(["abcdefg"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()))
>>> a.str.find("d", -6, -3)
0    2
dtype: int64[pyarrow]
>>>
```


### Issue Description

Expected result is 3.

### Expected Behavior

>>> "abcdefg".find("d", -6, -3)
3
>>>
Expected result is 3.

review_comments: Both pd.StringDtype() and python str.find allow start to be None.

1. What happens when `start` would wrap around a string entry e.g. `start=16` here
2. What would happen if `start=-3, end=-6`?

Added test cases for both to verify -1 is produced (same as builtin python str.find and pd.StringDtype()), it should work since we look for the substring after slicing the original string by start/end, so in both cases, slice_codeunits slices off the whole string, so there's no match.

Looking at code again, this approach doesn't handle case where sub is empty string correctly. I think a different approach should be used that avoids substring, going to mark as a draft, and refactor, and add tests for empty string case.

I've adjusted the code to handle empty strings as the substring, I also added test_str_find_e2e, that enumerates multiple combinations and baselines against the python str.find, I believe and e2e test is the best way to test this, manually picking a few cases is unlikely to cover all cases for this API, there are too many interesting cases.
Any chance you've looked at using a slice object here already? It feels like that could help simplify a lot of the branching being done here for things being None / 0

I don't think a slice object would help here, since I believe for this method, we need a positive start index, to calculate the offset of the substring from the original string. This PR essentially converts start into equivalent, but positive index, then it can be added to the resulting index returned by pc.find_substring. For example, if string is "abc" and start is -1, we calculate start_offset as 2, which is the equivalent positive index. We can use this offset to find the index of the substring in the original string, by adding it the position of the substring result.
